2 1 Executive Summary In order to strengthen the Union’s rules for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) aims to harmonise the preventative measures to be put in place at Union level.

To this end, Article 28(1) AMLR mandates the Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AMLA) to develop draft Regulatory Technical Standards specifying, among others, the requirements and information to be collected for standard customer due diligence, simplified due diligence (SDD) and enhanced due diligence (EDD) purposes.

The mandate also requires AMLA to specify risk factors that supervisors must consider when determining the extent to which certain electronic money instruments may be exempted from some customer due diligence (CDD) measures and which reliable and independent sources of information obliged entities may use to verify the identity of natural or legal persons for the purposes of Article 22(6) and (7) AMLR. The mandate further covers the attributes which electronic identification means, and relevant qualified trust services referred to in Article 22(6), point (b), AMLR must feature to fulfil the requirements of Article 20(1), points (a) and (b), AMLR in the case of standard, simplified and enhanced due diligence.

To frontload work on AMLA’s mandates before the effective operation of AMLA, the European Commission issued a Call for Advice (CfA) to the European Banking Authority (EBA) on 12 March 2024, requesting preparation of these regulatory technical standards under the mandate in Article 28(1) AMLR. The EBA issued its response to the CfA on 30 October 2025 which served as a strong foundation for AMLA to finalise the work.

In preparing this final report, AMLA sought and considered input from national supervisors across both financial and non-financial sectors, AMLA also liaised closely with private sector representatives. AMLA further enhanced the final report by considering the responses provided by respondents collected through the public consultation conducted between 9 February and 8 May 2026.

The draft RTS outlined in this final report contains proportionate, risk-based CDD measures that contribute to harmonising the way AML/CFT requirements are applied in the Union. The provisions are flexible enough to ensure applicability across the range of products and services offered by obliged entities in both the financial and non-financial sector. These draft RTS support simplification efforts and enable obliged entities to determine the most effective and proportionate measures to be applied. These draft RTS are part of a broader set of AMLA instruments that will be delivered and that will touch upon the AML/CFT requirements of obliged entities. AMLA will continue its endeavors to place proportionality and the risk-based approach at the heart of this work and ensure the effectiveness of the instruments to be delivered while simplifying AML/CFT compliance for obliged entities where possible.
1.1 Next steps These draft regulatory technical standards will be submitted to the European Commission for adoption before being published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

3 2 Background and rationale

2.1 Background In 2024, the European Union adopted a new package of laws to strengthen the EU's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) rules. With this package, the rules that apply to obliged entities are transferred to a directly applicable regulation, moving away from divergent national frameworks towards a single harmonised set of rules across the Union. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) sets out detailed requirements including on customer due diligence measures and suspicious transaction reporting and extends the application of AML/CFT rules to new categories of obliged entities.

To further ensure that customer due diligence (CDD) measures are applied in the same way, Article 28(1) AMLR requires the Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AMLA) to develop draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) setting out the requirements and information to be collected for standard customer due diligence, simplified due diligence (SDD) and enhanced due diligence (EDD) purposes. That mandate also requires AMLA to specify risk factors that supervisors must take into account when determining the extent to which certain electronic money instruments may be exempted from some customer due diligence measures and which reliable and independent sources of information obliged entities may use to verify the identity of natural or legal persons for the purposes of Article 22(6) and (7) AMLR. The mandate also specifies the attributes which electronic identification means, and relevant qualified trust services referred to in Article 22(6), point (b), AMLR must feature in order to fulfil the requirements of Article 20(1), points (a) and (b), of the AMLR in the case of standard, simplified and enhanced due diligence.

On 12 March 2024, the European Commission asked the European Banking Authority (EBA) by way of a Call for Advice (CfA) to prepare the above-mentioned regulatory technical standards to support the rapid and effective start of AMLA. The CfA included a mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR on CDD. The process established by the EBA to deliver on the CfA included a 3-month public consultation as well as a public hearing in April 2025, which more than 600 stakeholders joined, mostly from the financial sector. Based on the written feedback provided by 170 respondents to the consultation as well as subsequent discussions, the EBA’s draft RTS that went out for public consultation were amended. The EBA submitted its response to the European Commission’s Call for Advice, on 30 October 2025 AMLA used EBA’s work as a basis to further refine the draft RTS, with a special attention given to the nonfinancial sector. A revised version of the draft was submitted to a three-month public consultation on 9 February 2026. 325 responses were received through the consultation process. On 24 March 2026, AMLA also held a public hearing in which AMLA staff engaged with more than 1 600 stakeholders from Member States and third countries. Associations and obliged entities from both the financial and nonfinancial sectors were represented during the public hearing.

To ensure greater insight into specific sectors, AMLA also set up targeted meetings with key stakeholders. AMLA also engaged with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS). Following the conclusion of the consultation process, AMLA further refined the draft RTS in light of the feedback received from respondents and stakeholders.

2.2 AMLA’s approach - focus on simplification In developing these draft RTS, and taking into account the outcome of the public consultation, AMLA built on the EBA’s five guiding principles1 to ensure continuity, whilst placing specific focus on simplification by minimizing complexity, regulatory burden and compliance costs. This means that AMLA sought to establish a single, horizontal applicable framework to obliged entities from the financial and non-financial sector by:
• ensuring that the draft RTS complement what is provided in the AMLR, without repeating the Level 1 provisions that are sufficiently detailed;
• ensuring that the draft RTS continue to allow flexibility by setting out options obliged entities can consider when deciding on the most effective and proportionate measures;

• confining modifications to the EBA’s text where duly justified, for example, where AMLA saw a need to enhance or add to an RTS provision proposed by the EBA to ensure a wider applicability to both the financial and the non-financial sector; and

• balancing the need to ensure continuity and respecting the agreement reached among competent authorities and the EBA, while ensuring the draft RTS reflects AMLA’s mandate and accountability, as well as the views of its stakeholders.

2.3 Rationale AMLA sought to ensure that the requirements in the EBA's draft RTS can be applied by all obliged entities, particularly those in the non-financial sector, which were outside the scope and focus of the EBA's work. To this end, AMLA engaged with supervisors of the non-financial sector, with a view to identifying sectoral specificities that may impact the harmonised application of CDD requirements. On this basis, AMLA did not identify a need for major adjustments in the structure or content of the draft RTS initially submitted by the EBA.
AMLA’s continuation of the work therefore focused on identifying any outstanding issues and assessing whether this would require adjustments to the draft RTS.

As part of this, AMLA explored whether CDD measures could be further simplified beyond the existing reduced measures already permitted under Article 33 AMLR. AMLA did not identify opportunities for further simplifying SDD measures without effectively creating exemptions from the AMLR obligations, which would exceed AMLA’s mandate.

The feedback received during the public consultation did not alter this assessment, nor did it identify any additional horizontally applicable SDD measures that could be specified in these draft RTS in a manner consistent with the AMLR. At the same time, AMLA recognises the importance of ensuring that the AMLR can be applied in a proportionate and operationally effective manner. Accordingly, AMLA intends to continue engaging with stakeholders, including in particular the non-financial sector, to assess whether additional guidance on the application of SDD measures would be warranted.

1 A proportionate, risk-based approach, a focus on effective, workable outcomes, technological neutrality, maximum harmonisation across supervisors, Member States and sectors, limiting disruption by building on existing EBA standards where possible, whilst aligning with global AML/CFT benchmarks.

5 In the final draft RTS, AMLA introduced targeted amendments to the EBA’s initial draft aimed at enhancing legal clarity, promote simplification, while ensuring the applicability of the requirements across both the financial and non-financial sectors, and strengthening consistency and alignment with the AMLR ensuring AMLA does not derogate from it. This also means that where concerns were raised by respondents regarding provisions in the AMLR, AMLA was not able to address them through these RTS.

The AML/CFT package mandates AMLA with the development of a broad set of legal instruments concerning the AML/CFT requirements of obliged entities. Together, these instruments support a more harmonised framework by aligning supervisory expectations and reducing cross-border divergences. In developing this work, AMLA places simplification and the risk-based approach at the heart of its approach, to ensure that rules are applied proportionately and effectively in combating money laundering and terrorist financing. Therefore, in revising these draft RTS, AMLA also considered their interaction with its other mandates to ensure consistency and coherence across the regulatory and supervisory framework, while supporting simplification and reducing compliance burden for obliged entities. This approach further promotes a more harmonized, proportionate and risk-based AML/CFT framework.

of XXX supplementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council with regard to regulatory technical standards specifying the information and requirements necessary for the performance of customer due diligence for the purposes of Article 28(1)

(Text with EEA relevance) THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION, Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Having regard to Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2024 on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing2, and in particular Article 28(1), points (a) to (e), thereof, Whereas:

(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 aims for the harmonisation of customer due diligence measures across Member States and obliged entities within the EU. To achieve this, this Commission Delegated Regulation (‘Regulation’) sets common parameters for the application of customer due diligence measures. Obliged entities are required to adjust the customer due diligence measures based on the money laundering and terrorist financing risks associated with their business relationships or occasional transactions. This will ensure a proportionate and effective approach. Accordingly, obliged entities shall collect information on a risk-sensitive basis and apply the measures laid down in this Regulation, ensuring that their scope, intensity and frequency are proportionate to the money laundering and terrorist financing risks associated with the business relationship or occasional transaction.

(2) Obliged entities should, when identifying a customer and verifying their identity, collect data and information in a consistent way in all Member States. The same approach should apply to all customers, whether they are a natural person or a legal person. However, certain identity details are indicated differently on identity documents, passports or equivalent documents, depending on the issuing designated authority. For instance, on some documents the place of birth is indicated by the city or state, while in others it is indicated by the country of birth. Similarly, middle names are not consistently featured in documents but may in some cases be a relevant part of an individual’s identity information. To this end, this Regulation should allow obliged entities to verify such information as it is indicated in the identity document, passport or equivalent, or as available through electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services as set out in Regulation (EU) No 910//2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on electronic identification and trust services for electronic transactions in the internal market and repealing Directive 1999/93/EC3. A document does not necessarily need to include a middle name for it to be compliant with the requirements of this Regulation. Where obliged

8 entities collect only the state, city, municipality, town, or village of birth, they should assess the need to also ascertain the country, for instance where the name of the city in question is not unique to one country and there are doubts as to the country of birth or where the country cannot be readily identified from the city name.

(3) In the course of their operations, some legal entities adopt trade names that differ from their legal name. Since such trade names do not typically hold the same legal status as the legal name of the entity, they are not mandatory components of the identification details for legal entities. However, such information may bear relevance for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) purposes and could contribute to improving risk mitigation, including screening. To this end, and even where such names are not verifiable against reliable and independent sources, obliged entities should collect them together with the identification details of the legal entity.

(4) Identity documents, passports or equivalent issued by a designated authority in accordance with the applicable law may not always contain all the identification information required for AML/CFT purposes. For instance, passports do not typically include a residential address. In such cases, and where verification of the address is required, obliged entities must take measures to verify such information using reliable and independent sources. However, obliged entities need not request additional documents to verify information that has already been verified through the identification documents issued by a designated authority in accordance with the applicable law, as this would entail the unnecessary duplication and processing of data.

(5) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires obliged entities to identify senior managing officials in certain situations where no beneficial owner can be identified. Recital 125 of that Regulation explains that, although identified as such, senior managing officials are not the beneficial owners. Since those persons act in their capacity as officials of the legal entity rather than for their direct personal benefit, and to minimise the processing of personal data, it should be sufficient to identify the registered office address of the legal entity rather than the residential address of those senior managing officials.

(6) Obliged entities are expected to identify the nationalities held by a customer or beneficial owner. However, to establish whether a person holds any additional nationalities to those already identified and verified, obliged entities would, in most cases, have to rely on a declaration from the customer or beneficial owner. To this end, this Regulation only requires taking reasonable measures to identify any additional nationalities; and in the case of multiple nationalities, verifying one nationality will be sufficient. In situations where the person is stateless or has refugee or subsidiary protection status, this information should be obtained instead.

(7) Information or data collected by obliged entities for customer due diligence purposes may not always be in the form of documents. This Regulation specifies the situations where documents should be collected.

(8) For a document to be considered equivalent to an identity document or passport, it should give obliged entities sufficient reassurance of a person’s identity. Therefore, this Regulation sets out the minimum conditions, including the information and security features. Those security features may be based on international standards such as those set out in Part 2 of the International Civil Aviation Organization Document 9303. In order to ensure the reliability and integrity of identity verification processes, it is also appropriate for documents obtained for the purpose of verifying the identity of a natural person to be subject to checks for authenticity, including to ascertain that they have not been forged or otherwise tampered with.

(9) Obtaining data and documents from independent and reliable sources is key to ensuring that obliged entities can be satisfied that they know who their customers are. Reliable and independent sources of information for customers that are not natural persons include, but are not limited to statutory documents of the legal entity or legal arrangement required by law, including certificates of incorporation or audited financial statements; the most recent version of the constitutive documents establishing the legal entity or legal arrangement, including a memorandum of association and articles of association, or a recent official copy or extract of these documents issued by the applicable public registers and lists or an unofficial copy thereof certified by an independent professional or a public authority. In the case of a trust or similar legal arrangement that may not be subject to registration, a recent copy of the trust deed or an extract thereof, together with any other document that determines the exercise of any powers by the trustees or similar administrators, certified by an independent professional, could qualify as a reliable and independent source of information. Obliged entities should also take into account the recency of a document and whether the passage of time has reduced the reliability of that information. It should be left to the obliged entity to determine the most appropriate method for ensuring they understand information in a foreign language.

(10) There may be situations where the customer does not hold an identity document(s), passport(s) or equivalent that meets all the conditions set out in this Regulation. This could be the case where the customer has credible and legitimate reasons for being unable to provide traditional forms of identity documentation, for example being an asylum seeker; a refugee; a person to whom a residence permit was not granted but whose repatriation is impossible for legal or factual reasons; being homeless; or being otherwise vulnerable. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 does not provide an exemption from the list of information obliged entities should collect for natural persons in this category. To mitigate the risk of financial exclusion and unwarranted de-risking, obliged entities should be able to obtain the requested information from these natural persons via other reliable and independent means. This could be the case where the customer is or acts on behalf of a minor who does not possess a passport or identity document. In view of the minor’s representation by a parent or legal guardian, who would themselves be subject to identification and verification, it would be appropriate to consider a birth certificate as a credible source for the purposes of identifying and verifying the identity of the minor. In situations where a verified copy of the identity document, passport or equivalent is required, it should be attested that the copy corresponds to the original document.

(11) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires obliged entities to verify identity through identity documents, passports or equivalent or through certain electronic identification solutions set out in Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. Those electronic identification solutions comprise electronic identification means as defined in Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, regardless of whether they are notified under Article 9 of that Regulation or not, as long as they comply with the requirements of either ‘substantial’ or ‘high’ assurance levels, as specified in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1502 of 8 September 2015 on setting out minimum technical specifications and procedures for assurance levels for electronic identification means pursuant to Article 8(3) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council on electronic identification and trust services for electronic transactions in the internal market4. This includes European Digital Identity Wallets. Those electronic identification solutions also comprise relevant qualified trust services as defined in Article 3(17) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. While the electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services described above should
F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4

10 be used wherever possible, there may be situations where none of them can be used. This may occur where the customer cannot reasonably be expected to present identification documents in person and the customer cannot use the electronic identification solutions referred to above in Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. To ensure that such persons are not excluded and that financial or commercial services can continue to be provided, this Regulation enables the use of alternative verification measures through other means, taking advantage of developments in digital identity verification technologies. Such alternative solutions should nevertheless meet minimum requirements regarding the quality, security and confidentiality of the verification process, especially in the face of emerging technological threats. In these situations, obliged entities may continue using existing remote onboarding tools that meet those requirements. As such alternative solutions should only be used on a case-by-case basis where customers cannot be verified through either of the methods set out in Article 22(6) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, obliged entities should be required to justify instances of verification through such tools. Obliged entities may choose to demonstrate compliance with the minimum requirements through adherence to recognised international or European technical standards. Verification through electronic identification means or relevant qualified trust services need not be limited to non-face-toface situations, and obliged entities should be able to use such means when verifying the customer’s identity in person.

(12) Obtaining beneficial owner information for all customers that are not natural persons is essential for complying with AML/CFT requirements and with targeted financial sanctions obligations. For this reason, consultation of central registers for information on the beneficial owners is necessary. Central registers can be a source of information for the identification of the beneficial owner but are not sufficient on their own to fulfil the verification requirements.

(13) The process of verifying that a person purporting to act on behalf of a customer is authorised to do so enables obliged entities to confirm that such person has legal or juridical representation of the customer or any other similar power to legally bind the customer. Where the customer is a legal entity, such persons could include the legal representatives, signatories or similar persons that seek to exercise such powers with regard to the customer. On the other hand, the authority to act on behalf of a natural person could be verified through instruments such as power of attorney or proof of legal or parental representation, including a court-appointed guardianship.

(14) Understanding the purpose and intended nature of a business relationship or occasional transaction enables obliged entities to develop a holistic understanding of the customer. This allows them to assess whether the service or product requested is aligned with the customer’s profile and to conduct meaningful ongoing monitoring. To this end, the type and amount of information collected may vary depending on the product or service and should be proportionate to the risks sought to be mitigated. This also means that certain information will not always be relevant. Information on the source of funds, where needed, may provide reassurance that the funds to be used are derived from a legitimate source. However, the extent of information needed on the source of funds, if at all, should be commensurate to the risk to be mitigated. To avoid unnecessary processing of information, obliged entities should consider whether information already at their disposal contributes to understanding the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or occasional transaction.

(15) Article 20(1), point (h), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires that obliged entities identify and verify the identity of the natural person on whose behalf or for the benefit of whom a transaction or activity is being conducted. This Regulation lays down specific rules for the identification and verification of the identity of the final investors of a collective
F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4

11 investment undertaking that distributes its shares or units through another credit or financial institution, which acts in its own name but on behalf or for the benefit of one or more final investors. To ensure the effectiveness of customer due diligence measures and the proportionality of their application, it is appropriate to allow collective investment undertakings, where the relationship with the intermediary institution is not assessed as posing a high risk, to rely on that institution for the identification and verification of the final investors, provided that strict conditions are met.

(16) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires specific measures to be applied to transactions or business relationships with politically exposed persons (PEPs). The focus of this Regulation is on measures for the identification, by obliged entities of PEPs, their family members or persons known to be close associates. PEP screening measures should apply to the customer, its beneficial owner and the person on whose behalf or for the benefit of whom a transaction or activity is being carried out. These measures are important because once a PEP, family member or person known to be close associate is identified, the obliged entity should apply specific and additional customer due diligence measures in relation to that customer.
(17) Simplified due diligence measures should ease the administrative burden on obliged entities and on their customers and allow obliged entities to focus efforts where risks are higher.

(18) Minimum requirements for the identification of natural persons in low-risk situations should include at least the type of information that is usually included in a passport or identity document. As such, this Regulation permits that in situations of low risk, obliged entities are not required to collect and verify the address of the natural person. This ensures that obliged entities have sufficient and verifiable information to establish the identity of their customers, while keeping the requirements proportionate to the low level of money laundering / terrorism financing risk.

(19) This Regulation specifies the minimum information to identify the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or occasional transaction in low-risk situations. When assessing the purpose and intended nature in such situations, there may be situations in which the risk-based approach still requires obliged entities to determine whether any additional information, such as the source of funds, is needed to mitigate specific risks.

(20) In situations where the money laundering / terrorism financing risks are higher, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 calls for the application of enhanced due diligence measures to manage and mitigate these risks appropriately. These measures apply in addition to the customer due diligence measures laid down in Article 20 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. Where obliged entities obtain additional information in relation to the measures referred to in Article 34(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, to meet these requirements and mitigate the higher risk appropriately and effectively, that information should be of sufficient quality to enable an assessment of the authenticity and accuracy of the information already held on the customer and to inform the overall assessment of the business relationship or occasional transaction.

(21) Additional information obliged entities obtain to understand customers’ and beneficial owners’ source of funds and source of wealth in high-risk situations should enable them to satisfy themselves that the funds and assets used by the customer and beneficial owners are of legitimate origin.

(22) There may be situations where the information to be collected under Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and this Regulation is already available to the obliged entity or, for example, to other obliged entities within the group. This could also be the case when information is obtained, for instance, to understand the customer's investment profile, insurance needs,
F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4

12 the nature of the engagement or as part of the audit acceptance process. Where this is the case, obliged entities should consider how such information contributes to complying with their AML/CFT requirements, such as understanding the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or occasional transaction, before requesting similar information to avoid unnecessary duplication and reduce the regulatory burden on both the obliged entity and its customers. Where existing information is not deemed sufficient, additional information should be obtained.

(23) Customer due diligence measures include a specific requirement for obliged entities to verify whether the customer or the beneficial owner is subject to targeted financial sanctions as defined by Article 2(49) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. Screening for the application of trade or economic sanctions, such as arms embargoes, trade restrictions or travel bans, falls outside the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and, consequently, of this Regulation.

(24) Article 19(7) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 provides a list of four conditions on the basis of which AML/CFT supervisors may decide to grant an exemption for electronic money issuers from the customer due diligence measures in Article 20(1), points (a), (b) and (c), of that Regulation. To enable supervisors to determine the extent of such exemption (i.e. ‘in full or in part’) in a consistent way across Member States, this Regulation provides AML/CFT supervisors with a non-exhaustive list of risk factors associated with features of electronic money instruments.

(25) This Regulation sets out the minimum attributes that electronic identification means or qualified trust services must include to enable the identification and verification of the identity of a person for customer due diligence purposes. Some data points are only required when they are available, such as certain elements of an address, and certain data points are not relevant in all situations, for example data points concerning legal entities are not relevant when the customer is a natural person. The electronic identification means or qualified trust services used must nevertheless enable the capture of the minimum attributes specified in Annex I in structured data fields, so that obliged entities can verify a broad range of customers. This does not mean that obliged entities using electronic identification means or qualified trust services should identify and verify a larger set of data than the identification data required under this Regulation or Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(26) Obliged entities need to ensure that their customer information remains up to date. The maximum periods of 1 and 5 years respectively for updating customer information in accordance with the requirements of Article 26(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 should only start with the date of entry into force of this Commission Delegated Regulation for ongoing business relationships established before that date.

(27) To allow obliged entities sufficient time to adapt, where necessary, their systems, policies, controls and procedures, including training of staff, to the requirements laid down in this Regulation, and thereby facilitate their effective implementation, this Regulation should apply six months after its entry into force.

(28) This Regulation is based on the draft regulatory technical standards submitted to the Commission by the Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (the ‘Authority’).

SECTION 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS Article 1 Proportionality and risk-based approach This Commission Delegated Regulation (‘Regulation’) shall be applied in line with the risk-based approach. The extent and the nature of the information to be obtained and the measures to be applied by obliged entities shall be proportionate to the type and level of risk identified and shall enable obliged entities to manage and mitigate that risk appropriately, including through the application of simplified due diligence measures in situations of low risk. SECTION 2 INFORMATION TO BE COLLECTED FOR IDENTIFICATION AND VERIFICATION PURPOSES Article 2 Information to be obtained in relation to names

1. In relation to the names and surnames of a natural person as referred to in Article 22(1), point (a)(i), and Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, obliged entities shall obtain all names, including first name(s) (given name(s)) and surname(s) (family name(s)) that feature on the identity document, passport or equivalent or through the electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services referred to in Article 22(6), point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

2. In relation to the name of a legal entity as referred to in Article 22(1), point (b)(i), or other organisations that have legal capacity under national law as referred to in Article 22(1), point (d)(i), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, obliged entities shall obtain the legal name and, where applicable, the trade name where it differs from the legal name. Article 3 Information to be obtained in relation to address
1. The information on the address as referred to in Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 shall consist of the following information:

4.1 Impact assessment with cost-benefit analysis Introduction As per Article 49(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620, before submitting draft regulatory technical standards to the European Commission, AMLA shall conduct open public consultations and analyse the potential related costs and benefits.
This analysis presents the Impact assessment with cost-benefit analysis (IA/CBA) of the main policy options included in the draft RTS on CDD under Article 28(1) AMLR.

This IA/CBA is qualitative and quantitative in nature. The policy choices have been taken primarily in accordance with qualitative considerations, taking into account the experience and professional judgment of supervisors from the financial and the non-financial sectors, self-regulatory bodies (SRBs), and the European Commission.

In addition, the analysis was complemented with evidence collected through the public consultation conducted between 9 February and 8 May 2026. This included, among other, information from obliged entities regarding the expected one-off implementation and recurring costs associated with the draft RTS. While the quantitative evidence is based on stakeholders’ estimates and does not constitute a comprehensive assessment of costs across all obliged entities, it provides a useful indication of the expected financial and resource implications of the draft RTS. Where quantitative evidence remained limited or unavailable, the analysis is supported by structured qualitative reasoning and professional judgement informed by supervisory experience and stakeholders’ input.

A. Problem identification CDD requirements are essential to ensure that obliged entities identify and verify their customers and monitor their business relationships, in relation to the money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF) risks that they pose. It is therefore necessary to achieve a uniform and high-standard application of CDD measures in the Union, relying on harmonised requirements, amongst others, for the identification of customers and verification of their identity, as well as identification of the purpose and intended nature of the business relationships and occasional transactions. This ensures the consistent application of the provisions throughout the Union, thus allowing for a level-playing field across sectors and within the internal market. At the same time, it is essential that obliged entities apply CDD measures in a riskbased manner.

Under the previous EU AML/CFT framework, relying heavily on the national implementation of EU requirements, notably Directive (EU) 2015/849 and its amendments, the effective prevention of ML/TF was hampered due to divergent interpretations of the AML/CFT framework across Member States. Although the earlier framework sought to ensure equivalent safeguards, the national discretion in transposing the CDD requirements resulted in regulatory divergences that created legal uncertainty and additional costs for obliged entities operating on a cross-border basis, regulatory arbitrage risks, and uneven levels of protection against ML/TF within the internal market.

31 To address these shortcomings, the AMLR introduces harmonised, directly applicable rules, including CDD obligations that are uniform throughout the Union and across sectors. This ensures that obliged entities are subject to the same standards for requirements such as customer and beneficial ownership identification and verification, and ongoing monitoring.

The AMLR also broadens the scope of obliged entities within the AML/CFT framework, introducing new categories that were not previously subject to AML/CFT requirements, including CDD measures. These include crowdfunding service providers, investment migration operators, football clubs and agents, credit intermediaries for mortgage and consumer credits, non-financial mixed activity holding companies, as well as types of crypto-asset service providers and traders in certain high-value goods, the latter of which were considered obliged entities under the previous framework within narrower aspects of their business activities. By expanding the list of obliged entities, the Regulation seeks to address emerging ML/FT risks in the financial and non-financial sectors by ensuring that gatekeepers to the financial system are in a position to protect the internal market from criminal misuse. To ensure that all obliged entities have a clear understanding of CDD requirements and apply those obligations consistently and according to a risk-based approach, Article 28(1) AMLR requires AMLA to develop draft RTS on CDD.

B. Policy objectives The overarching objective of this mandate is to further ensure the consistent, proportionate, and harmonised application of CDD measures by all obliged entities in the EU, drawing upon the experience and support of supervisors in the financial and non-financial sectors.

More specifically, these draft RTS establish a harmonised framework specifying the information that obliged entities shall collect for the purpose of performing standard due diligence, including the information to be collected for identification and verification purposes and for identifying the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or the occasional transaction; the type of simplified due diligence (SDD) measures to be applied in case of lower risk; and the additional information to be collected for the purposes of enhanced due diligence (EDD).

The draft RTS also promote a consistent approach towards determining the extent of the exemption under Article 19(7) AMLR for certain electronic money instruments from CDD requirements, by specifying the risk factors associated with features of electronic money instruments that supervisors must take into account in that regard.

In addition, the draft RTS set out the reliable and independent sources of information for verifying the identification data of natural and legal persons and define the attributes that electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services must meet for the purposes of standard due diligence, SDD, and EDD.

Overall, the draft RTS aim to clarify and specify how certain obligations established by the AMLR should be applied, within the boundaries of the requirements imposed by the Regulation and without imposing additional obligations. The draft RTS aim to provide details where required by the legal mandate and where this brings added value for obliged entities, in line with the underlying principle of proportionality

32 and bearing in mind the need to ensure effectiveness in the fight against ML/TF without imposing unnecessary regulatory burden on the private sector.

As an overarching objective, the draft RTS contribute to the harmonised, risk-based goal of the AML/CFT package, by setting robust and consistent requirements that are at the same time proportionate and risk-based. The framework is designed to be technologically neutral and to achieve a high level of harmonisation, including sector-specific criteria where necessary.

C. Baseline scenario Under the baseline scenario, obliged entities would apply the CDD obligations as set out in Chapter III of the AMLR. The relevant provisions in that Regulation are more detailed than those of the currently applicable Directive, enabling a greater degree of harmonisation in the Union. However, the level of detail, particularly on the information to be collected, is not sufficient to guarantee the consistent and effective application of those CDD measures. These gaps may give rise to different supervisory approaches and expectations, which would continue to pose a regulatory burden on obliged entities that operate across borders. Where rules are not sufficiently clear, there is an additional risk that obliged entities apply different standards and their supervisors have different supervisory expectations, creating an uneven playing field across the Union.

Furthermore, the AMLR grants supervisors discretion to exempt certain electronic money instruments from some of the CDD rules, subject to a proven low risk. The AMLR requires AMLA to specify the risk factors that supervisors should take into account when determining the extent of that exemption. In the absence of a commonly agreed set of minimum risk factors, supervisors might apply divergent criteria. This may create an uneven landscape in which some Member States base their decisions on a narrower set of risk factors than others or otherwise fail to take important risks into account. Given that an exemption granted by one national supervisor has implications across the internal market, Member States must have a degree of reassurance on the exemptions granted within the Union. A common set of minimum risk factors is needed to reach these objectives.

Finally, technological innovation in the area of qualified trust services and electronic identification could be hampered by uncertainty on the attributes that such solutions should feature if they are to be compliant for verification purposes.

33 Background Article 28(1) AMLR requires AMLA to develop draft RTS on CDD, in line with the overall objective to introduce directly applicable rules that ensure the consistent, proportionate, and harmonised application of CDD measures by all obliged entities in the EU.

To lay the ground for the development of this important mandate before AMLA’s establishment, on 12 March 2024 the European Commission issued a Call for Advice to EBA. To prepare its response, the EBA established a drafting process involving experts from 60 EU AML/CFT supervisors. Given the EBA’s remit on the financial sector, most of the supervisors involved were responsible for the financial sector, but some were supervising both the financial and non-financial sectors. The EBA also engaged closely with the European Commission, the other European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs), and AMLA, once established. In addition, the EBA engaged with the private sector and consumer groups, the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) Platform, the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and the EDPS. The process also included a 3-month public consultation as well as a public hearing, which more than 600 stakeholders joined. The draft RTS that went out for public consultation were amended, based on the written feedback provided by 170 respondents, mostly belonging to the financial sector, but also the non-financial sector albeit to a lesser extent, as well as feedback from the EDPB and EDPS. The EBA submitted its response to the European Commission’s Call for Advice on 30 October 2025. The response was formally delivered to AMLA immediately after that. In line with its mandate, the EBA’s response focused on the financial sector.

In parallel, to specifically address the needs of the non-financial sector, the European Commission set up an informal subgroup of its Expert Group on Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing (EGMLTF) comprising representatives of non-financial supervisors, to complement the EBA’s work with sectorspecific input, where needed. The outcome of this exercise was formally handed over to AMLA in September 2025.
Through this work the European Commission provided technical advice to facilitate AMLA’s delivery of the mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR.

Building on this work, AMLA reviewed and, where needed, amended the EBA’s draft RTS, taking into consideration the European Commission’s input regarding the non-financial sectors, and input collected from other stakeholders representing both the financial and the non-financial sectors. Overarching principles Overall, in line with the objectives set out in the AMLR, the draft RTS aim to ensure a high level of harmonisation across Member States and sectors, while preserving flexibility for obliged entities to apply a risk-based approach.
In particular, AMLA sought to preserve and promote the risk-based approach, focusing on effective, workable outcomes within the parameters of the AMLR.

The policy decisions also adhere to the principle of proportionality. This means that the draft RTS aim to define obligations that are suitable and necessary to achieve the desired outcomes, and do not impose additional burden on the obliged entities that is excessive in relation to the objective pursued.

In addition, AMLA ensured to be unbiased by considering the perspective of the different obliged entities to which this regulatory product is addressed, giving equal importance to the interests and needs of the obliged entities that are impacted at the same level, regardless of whether they operate in the financial or the non-financial sector.

The principle of technological neutrality was also respected, for example in relation to the measures related to verification of the identity on a non-face-to-face basis, as well as the screening requirements for the identification of politically exposed persons and the screening of customers and beneficial owners against targeted financial sanctions.

Lastly, AMLA aimed to ensure continuity of the regulatory framework by building on the work already undertaken and validated by the EBA and its AML/CFT stakeholders, while also taking into account further input from AMLA’s stakeholders in both the financial and non-financial sectors. Changes to the EBA’s proposed text were therefore limited to duly justified cases. Policy issue 1: Applicability and proportionality to the financial and non-financial sectors In its response to the European Commission's Call for Advice, the EBA highlighted that several of the provisions set out in the proposed draft RTS apply to obliged entities in the non-financial sector in the same manner as they apply to institutions in the financial sector. At the same time, considering the significant differences between the financial and non-financial sectors in terms of business models, operation, AML/CFT capacity and compliance maturity, the EBA suggested that AMLA may wish to assess the need for separate, standalone RTS on CDD measures for the non-financial sector. Therefore, the first decision made by AMLA focused on assessing the cross-sectoral applicability of the draft RTS developed by the EBA and their proportionality on non-financial sector obliged entities. In that context, AMLA considered the following options:
A. Adopting a sector-specific approach, by developing two separate draft RTS for the financial and the non-financial sectors.
B. Adopting a horizontal approach, by issuing one single draft RTS setting flexible, horizontal provisions, complemented with limited, targeted sector-specific measures only where necessary.

35 Option A Under Option A, two distinct draft RTS would be developed, one applicable to the financial sector and one to the non-financial sector, including specific provisions reflecting identified differences in business models, risk exposure, and operational needs.
Benefits
• This approach would allow for tailored CDD requirements, closely aligned with sector specificities and operational realities.

• It would also allow for more tailored expectations by requiring the use of specific sources or types of documents, which could be useful especially for those obliged entities which have been subject to CDD requirements for the first time under the new AML/CFT framework.
• This may reduce the need for interpretative guidance at a later stage for sectors with very specific business models and operational needs.

• Sector-specific draft RTS might be easier to apply for some categories of obliged entities, particularly those that are different to traditional credit and financial institutions, as more tailored and prescriptive provisions may limit the room for interpretation in the practical application of specific measures.
Costs

• This approach risks undermining the risk-based approach that underpins an effective AML/CFT regime. The specific rules may reduce the discretion left to obliged entities to determine which measures, including information and documents to be collected, are most appropriate to address the specific risk posed by a given business relationship or occasional transaction. This would in turn reduce the opportunity to focus on resources where risks are higher. This may also reduce an obliged entity’s ability to apply measures that are equally or more effective than those specified in the draft RTS.

• When considering that both the financial and non-financial sectors present a certain level of heterogeneity in their subsectors, the rationale for having one instrument for the financial sector and another instrument for the non-financial sector becomes less clear.

• Moreover, separate instruments will likely result in different rules for the same requirements. As the CDD requirements (e.g., understanding the ownership and control structure) do not inherently change by sector, there is no obvious, substantial justification for requiring different information and documents to be collected for the financial and non-financial sectors.

• In line with the previous point, this approach would aggravate regulatory fragmentation, thus undermining the harmonisation objective pursued by the AMLR and creating an unlevel playing field across Member States and sectors, ultimately increasing the risk of inconsistent application of CDD measures across the Union.

• The separation of the draft RTS might also lead to higher compliance costs for obliged entities operating across both the financial and non-financial sectors, which would need to comply with varying regulatory requirements. In practice, this would entail the development and maintenance of parallel internal policies and procedures, additional legal analysis and compliance oversight, higher training and adaptation costs, and would ultimately increase operational complexity.

Given that core CDD measures under Level 1 are largely identical across sectors, introducing two separate draft RTS for the financial and the non-financial sector would create unnecessary and unjustified complexity. Option B Under Option B, a single draft RTS would apply to both the financial and non-financial sectors, establishing common CDD requirements, with proportionality and flexibility embedded through riskbased application rather than sector-specific rules. Benefits
• In line with the objective of the AMLR, this approach would promote harmonisation and support the level-playing field, by ensuring consistency and legal clarity across all obliged entities.

• A common draft RTS would adhere to the risk-based approach, by setting horizontally applicable CDD requirements which can be applied in a flexible way to address the level and nature of the ML/TF risk identified, rather than differentiating rules according to the sector in which the obliged entity operates.

• This approach would also allow the draft RTS to address clearly identified and duly justified sectoral specificities, increasing legal certainty for obliged entities with specific operational needs.

• Horizontally applicable provisions would be future proof, being flexible enough for obliged entities to respond to emerging and evolving ML/TF risks and allow them to determine the extent, method and type of information or documents needed to mitigate the ML/TF risks they identify, regardless of sector, product or service.

• For obliged entities operating cross-sectoral, this approach would foster simplification and reduce implementation and compliance costs, as the same flexible requirements would apply regardless of sector, product offered, or service provided.
Costs

• The objective to provide legal certainty might not always be achieved, since some entities might face interpretative challenges in applying horizontal rules to very sector-specific business models. This might lead to increased compliance costs for obliged entities, along with increasing the risk of neglectful application due to misinterpretation.

Overall impact assessment and cost-benefit analysis Based on the assessments described above, these draft RTS adopt a horizontal approach with targeted sector-specific measures where necessary (Option B), with one single regulatory instrument setting flexible, horizontal provisions and requirements, complemented with limited, targeted sector-specific measures.

The draft RTS are designed to be consistent with the risk-based approach of the AMLR, requiring obliged entities to scale the extent and depth of CDD measures according to ML/TF risks, including those arising out of the business model and customer type. Input from supervisors in the financial and non-financial sectors indicated that principle-based draft RTS provide sufficient flexibility to accommodate sectoral differences in most cases, and that a horizontal framework supports legal certainty, particularly for obliged entities operating across multiple sectors or jurisdictions. Applying the same core CDD principles across sectors also ensures regulatory coherence and reduces the risk of divergent interpretations and expectations across sectors.

Feedback from supervisors also suggests that CDD challenges are not primarily sector-specific but risk specific, meaning that the determining factor should be the risk posed by the customer and the transaction, and the application of proportionate, risk-based CDD measures, rather than the sector in which the obliged entity operates (i.e., same risk, same rules).

Based on feedback from non-financial supervisors, while in certain cases sectoral specificities in the non-financial sectors translate into specific regulatory requirements at national level, those needs cannot be addressed within this mandate. Since those rules mainly reflect operational differences, AMLA expects that the new, harmonised framework will address many of the divergent practices and divergent supervisory expectations, and any remaining divergence would be better addressed through targeted interpretative guidance rather than differentiated obligations.

This decision acknowledges that some newly introduced obliged entities, particularly in parts of the non-financial sector, may incur initial compliance costs in interpreting how horizontal CDD principles apply to their specific business models, mainly associated with internal legal analysis, policy updates, and staff training. However, many of these costs would arise from the application of the AMLR on its own, independently of the draft RTS. Moreover, such costs are expected to be counterbalanced by an increase in the effectiveness of the application of CDD measures over time and would be justified by the objective pursued.

In line with the simplification and burden reduction objectives, these draft RTS adopt a streamlined approach, avoiding excessive detail and supporting sector compliance on a risk-based basis. Overall, the benefits outweigh the costs. Principle-based, horizontal provisions ensure harmonisation and legal certainty, while avoiding the significant administrative and compliance burden that would

Methodology The assessment of the policy options underpinning these draft RTS was informed by a combination of supervisory expertise, comparative legal analysis and stakeholder feedback obtained through the public consultation.

The assessment drew on structured exchanges with experts from supervisors responsible for the supervision of both financial and non-financial sectors. These discussions focused on supervisory experience with the application of CDD requirements across different sectors and business models, taking into account:
• the diversity of business models and risk exposures;
• observed challenges in applying horizontal, risk-based CDD obligations in practice;
• supervisory expectations regarding proportionality and scalability of CDD measures;
• the potential compliance and supervisory implications of sector-specific versus principlebased regulatory approaches;
• provisions that have proven effective and operationally workable in practice;
• areas where divergent interpretations or supervisory practices have emerged;
• the impact of the draft RTS proposed by the EBA on compliance costs and supervisory convergence; and
• the extent to which the EBA’s text can accommodate the expanded scope of obliged entities under the new framework.

The assessment also included a comparative legal analysis of the AMLR, notably the use of horizontal AML/CFT obligations applicable across both the financial and non-financial sectors, as well as AMLA's mandate under that Regulation. This analysis aimed to ensure that the draft RTS remain consistent with the underlying legislative framework, support regulatory coherence and avoid introducing unnecessary divergences that could undermine legal certainty or effective implementation or supervision.

Limitations The analysis is primarily based on qualitative evidence derived from structured exchanges with supervisors from the financial and non-financial sectors and comparative legal analysis, complemented by a qualitative and quantitative assessment of the feedback provided through the public consultation.

While supervisory experience and comparative legal analysis provide valuable insights into the practical application of the draft RTS, they may not capture all sector-specific particularities across the highly heterogeneous financial and non-financial sectors. In addition, supervisory practices and market structures continue to evolve, particularly in relation to newly designated obliged entities. These limitations are mitigated by the principle-based design of the draft RTS and the possibility of addressing any emerging issues through interpretative tools, where necessary.

As regards the evidence collected through the public consultation, it was provided voluntarily by respondents and may therefore not be fully representative of all categories of obliged entities or of the broader market. In addition, the number of respondents providing sufficiently substantiated cost assessments was relatively limited compared with the diversity and overall population of obliged entities affected by the draft RTS. Furthermore, the expected costs reported by respondents may vary depending on the size, business model, level of AML/CFT maturity, and existing AML/CFT compliance framework of the obliged entity. Lastly, while respondents were asked to assess the additional implementation costs attributable to the draft RTS beyond those arising from Chapter III of AMLR, distinguishing between the two regulatory instruments proved challenging. As a result, the cost estimates provided may also reflect implementation costs associated with compliance with the new requirements arising directly from Regulation itself.

4.2 Feedback on the public consultation On 9 February 2026 AMLA launched a public consultation on the Draft Regulatory Technical Standards under Article 28(1) AMLR. The consultation lasted 3 months and ended on 8 May 2026. A total of 325 responses were received. In terms of stakeholder representation, 23% of responses were submitted by industry associations representing the financial sector and 14% originated from industry associations representing the non-financial sector, followed by 21% from obliged entities of the financial sector, 13% from obliged entities of the non-financial sector, 5% from SRBs, 4 % from civil societies and the remainder from others.

This section presents the summary of the key issues and views raised by the respondents, details AMLA’s assessment of the responses, and concludes with AMLA’s decision regarding potential amendments to the final draft RTS.
4.2.1 SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES AND AMLA’S RESPONSE

1) Risk-based approach and flexibility Respondents from the financial and non-financial sector raised concerns that some requirements, notably those containing lists of information to be collected for identifying the purpose and intended nature of a business relationship or occasional transaction, verification of the beneficial owner and for enhanced due diligence, might be interpreted as too prescriptive and requiring the systematic collection and verification of information irrespective of the ML/TF risk exposure. Respondents therefore stressed the need for greater clarity confirming that the provisions of the draft RTS should not be applied as mandatory checklists and that the extent of information gathered should remain commensurate with the risk profile.

While respondents broadly welcomed the objective of achieving more consistent customer due diligence standards, a significant number emphasised the need to retain flexibility and better reflect sector-specific business models, operational practices and challenges. Representatives of auditors, external accountants and tax advisers, notaries, lawyers and other independent legal professionals, real estate agents, gambling service providers, insurance undertakings and pension-related obliged entities highlighted practical challenges in applying certain requirements in the context of occasional transactions and the exercise of their professional activities. These respondents also sought greater recognition that relevant information that is already available through professional mandates, contractual arrangements, products, services or existing business relationships, may be used for CDD purposes, and requested greater clarity regarding the level of detail expected when complying with the requirements set out in former Article 18 (current Article 16) of the draft RTS. Respondents from several sectors commented that the draft RTS appeared to give preference to automated screening tools, while treating manual checks as a secondary or exceptional option. This concern was raised in relation to both former Article 19 (current Article 17), on the identification of politically exposed persons (PEPs), and former Article 30 (current Article 25) of the draft RTS, on targeted financial sanctions screening. The comments were particularly prominent among non-financial sector respondents, including gambling and casino operators, real estate agents, art market and auctionhouse stakeholders, notaries, lawyers, accountants and auditors. These respondents considered that the mandatory or quasi-mandatory use of automated tools could be disproportionate for smaller

Some respondents also pointed to a perceived inconsistency between former Articles 19 and 30 of the draft RTS, as former Article 19 expressly referred to proportionality-based manual checks whereas former Article 30 was perceived as less clear in this regard.

Several respondents also proposed simplified due diligence measures for specific products, sectors and categories of customers considered to present a low degree of ML/TF risks. Finally, respondents also commented on the enhanced due diligence provisions with one of the main concerns related to the scope of information that may be required in higher-risk situations.

AMLA’s response Avoiding excessive prescriptiveness was a key consideration for AMLA throughout the drafting of the RTS; for example, the text was revised to clarify that its provisions should not be interpreted as imposing checklist-based obligations instead, be implemented in a proportionate and risk-based manner, taking into account the specific circumstances of the obliged entity.

To address these concerns, AMLA strengthened Article 1 of the draft RTS to further emphasize that the RTS should be applied in a proportionate and risk-based manner. AMLA additionally introduced targeted amendments to Articles 10 and former 18 (current Article 16) of the draft RTS and certain enhanced due diligence provisions to specify that the scope of information and supporting documentation should remain commensurate with the ML/TF risks identified while maintaining the obliged entities' responsibility and supervisory discretion in case the information collected is not sufficient to mitigate the specific risks. While this approach reflects the discretion granted to obliged entities through the riskbased approach, it also clarifies that the information necessary should be determined on the basis of the ML/TF risks associated with the business relationship or occasional transaction, reducing unnecessary data requests and processing.

A recital already clarified that there may also be situations where the information to be collected under the AMLR and the draft RTS may already be available to the obliged entity or, for example, to other obliged entities within the group. AMLA specifies this further in the operative provisions and provides that information on the purpose and intended nature in low-risk situations may be inferred from the product or service.

To alleviate practical implementation challenges and to take into account divergences in identification documents, AMLA introduced greater flexibility on the collection of given names, place of birth information and nationalities, depending on the availability of that information. In the case of legal entities, AMLA also provided more flexibility with regard to the collection of trade names. Regarding the comments on former Articles 19 and 30 of the draft RTS, AMLA agrees that the use of screening measures should remain risk-based and technologically neutral, taking into account the size, nature, complexity and business model of the obliged entity. In particular, smaller obliged entities, entities with limited customer volumes, or entities carrying out occasional or low-volume activities should be able to rely on manual checks where those checks are sufficient to meet the relevant screening obligations. At the same time, the draft RTS must ensure that screening remains effective. Manual checks should

Obliged entities remain responsible for ensuring that the method chosen - whether automated, manual, or a combination of both - enables them to detect PEP or sanctions matches in a timely and effective manner. The amendments clarify that, under both former Article 19 and Article 30, obliged entities may use automated screening tools, manual checks, or a combination thereof. Manual checks are therefore no longer framed as an exceptional fallback, but as one of the available screening approaches where appropriate in light of the obliged entity’s circumstances.

AMLA did not deem it appropriate to introduce automatic simplified due diligence treatment for specific sectors, products or customer categories. This would run counter to the obliged entity’s requirement to assess individual risks under Article 20(2) AMLR. Nonetheless, with the amendments to Article 1 of the draft RTS AMLA does stress the application of simplified due diligence measures in situations presenting a low degree of risk.

In response to the feedback received, AMLA amended the provisions relating to EDD to make it clear that obliged entities have discretion to determine the appropriate measures in high-risk situations. This is consistent with the discretion that Article 34(4) AMLR grants to obliged entities to determine the appropriate EDD measures and in accordance with a targeted, tailored and risk-based approach. Through these targeted adjustments, AMLA aimed to further deliver on the risk-based approach and increase flexibility while maintaining compliance with the obligations set out in the AMLR.

2) Simplification A number of stakeholders questioned whether certain requirements in the draft RTS duplicated provisions already established in the AMLR or extended beyond the scope of the mandate conferred by Article 28(1) AMLR. Respondents also emphasised that some provisions did not provide sufficient additional regulatory value compared with those provisions in AMLR and risked creating legal uncertainty or operational complexity.

In this regard, respondents from the financial sector and the non-financial sector, in particular respondents from the real estate and legal sectors, questioned the treatment of senior managing officials under former Article 13 of the draft RTS. Several respondents argued that the requirement in the draft RTS could create uncertainty regarding the distinction between beneficial owners and senior managing officials and seemed to require the collection of information beyond what is set out in the AMLR.

Respondents across both the financial and non-financial sector, including notaries, also submitted feedback regarding the treatment of complex ownership and control structures and their relationship with ML/TF risk. A prevalent concern among them was that the criteria defining a complex structure in former Article 12 of the draft RTS captures an overly broad range of multi-layered ownership structures as inherently higher risk despite such structures often being established for commercial, regulatory or tax reasons. Consequently, stakeholders called for a more risk-based approach towards complexity indicators and their relationship with the higher-risk indicators set out in Annex III of AMLR.

49 AMLA’s response In carefully considering and assessing the responses received, AMLA has taken into account the scope of its mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR, as well as the need to maintain coherence with the existing legislative framework and avoid unnecessary duplication of regulatory provisions. To address concerns relating to senior managing officials, AMLA removed the former Article 13 from the draft RTS since the provision did not provide additional regulatory value and risked creating uncertainty regarding the distinction between beneficial owners and senior managing officials already established in the AMLR. Nonetheless, AMLA retained the core obligation to allow obliged entities to collect the registered office address of a senior managing official in the current Article 3(2) of the draft RTS. AMLA acknowledges the concerns raised regarding the treatment of ownership and control structures and the potential interpretation of structural complexity as an indicator of higher ML/TF risk. Therefore, AMLA moved away from a prescriptive definition of complex structures that automatically triggered certain mandatory measures to a more proportionate, risk-based approach. Consequently, AMLA merged former Articles 11 and 12 (current Article 11) of the draft RTS to allow obliged entities to assess the risk presented by a structure, while still laying out the characteristics that may contribute to complexity. This shifts some discretion back to obliged entities, who are best placed to determine whether a structure is indeed complex and how that impacts the business relationship or occasional transaction’s risk level. This approach acknowledges that complexity varies from one sector to another, and a large multinational structure may be standard for certain obliged entities, for instance company service providers or tax advisors, but complex for others that do not commonly encounter such structures.

AMLA considers that these amendments better reflect the scope of its mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR and reduce unnecessary duplication of provisions in the AMLR, thereby ensuring greater legal clarity and contributing to simplification.
